name: Transistor as GPT
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Tiny Switch That Rewrote Every Industry Twice
lesson.summary: The transistor shows what a general purpose technology looks like when its improvement curve, Moore's Law, runs unusually fast and unusually consistently for decades.
lesson.body:
The transistor is arguably the cleanest and fastest moving General Purpose Technology case in this book, and it is a useful one for seeing what a GPT looks like when the improvement over time test operates unusually fast and unusually consistently, compressing into a few decades a transformation that took the steam engine roughly a century and electricity several generations to fully deliver.

The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in December 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley, work that earned the three a shared Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956, replacing the bulkier, hotter, less reliable vacuum tube as the basic switching and amplifying component of electronics. Unlike a vacuum tube, a transistor has no filament to burn out, draws far less power, generates far less heat, and can be made smaller almost without limit, properties that mattered enormously once engineers began trying to pack millions and eventually billions of them onto a single chip.

Test two first, since it is the most dramatic part of this history: transistor improvement over time is captured by what became known as Moore's Law, Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors that could be economically packed onto an integrated circuit was roughly doubling on a regular cadence. That trend held, with adjustments to its exact pace, for decades, meaning the transistor did not arrive once and stay fixed. It kept becoming smaller, cheaper, and more power efficient at a pace with no real historical precedent, continually unlocking applications that were not economically possible even a few product generations earlier.

Test one, broad applicability: transistors, and the integrated circuits built from them, ended up in essentially every category of electronic device, computers, telecommunications switches, radios and televisions, industrial controls, medical devices, and eventually the microprocessors that run in nearly every modern object with a power switch, a breadth of application matched by very few other inventions in industrial history.

Test three, enabling further innovation, is arguably the transistor's strongest credential. It made the integrated circuit possible, which made the microprocessor possible, which made the personal computer, then the internet's underlying hardware, then the smartphone possible, an unbroken chain of complementary innovation stretching from a 1947 lab bench device to essentially all of modern computing, each layer depending on the transistor continuing to improve underneath it.

The transistor is a useful anchor case specifically because it shows what happens when a technology clears the science versus engineering gap unusually fast and then keeps improving reliably for decades: the payoff compounds instead of arriving as a single step change. When later chapters ask whether quantum computing might follow a similar improvement curve for its own basic unit, the qubit, this is the comparison being invoked, and it is a genuinely high bar, since not every GPT candidate gets a multi-decade, remarkably consistent improvement curve the way the transistor did.
